title: The stars of the Large Magellanic Cloud
caption: The globular cluster NGC 1854, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: White and blue stars gather in this Hubble image of NGC 1854, a globular cluster in the southern constellation of Dorado, the Dolphinfish. Its home, about 135 000 light-years away, is the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way and one of our nearest neighbors.

Stars are forming vigorously across the Large Magellanic Cloud. Well stocked with gas and dust, it holds approximately 60 globular clusters and 700 open clusters. Together with its smaller sibling, the Small Magellanic Cloud, it is the only system known to contain clusters at every stage of evolution, which makes its clusters popular subjects for research.

Hubble is often called on to study them. Its very high-resolution cameras can pick out individual stars even in a cluster's crowded core, revealing each cluster's mass, size and how far it has evolved. That lets astronomers compare clusters of many different ages side by side.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through visible (555 nm) and near-infrared (814 nm) filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves stars in another galaxy that no eye could separate.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The caption gives a distance of about 135 000 light-years, while catalog data lists about 140,000 light-years. The image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.
alt: A gathering of white and blue stars in a globular cluster.
